metin: The notion that creativity is the preserve of a gifted few has been steadily eroded by psychological research. Studies suggest that creative output depends less on innate genius than on sustained practice, broad exposure to ideas and a willingness to tolerate failure. Many celebrated innovators produced a large volume of mediocre work before achieving recognition. Seen in this light, creativity looks less like a rare spark and more like a skill that can be cultivated.
dogru: Research suggests that creativity is largely a skill developed through effort rather than an innate gift.
celdiriciler: Psychological research confirms that only a gifted minority can be truly creative.
Celebrated innovators rarely produced unsuccessful work before becoming famous.
Tolerating failure is shown to reduce creative output.

metin: Proponents of nuclear power argue that it offers a reliable, low-carbon source of electricity that could play a decisive role in tackling climate change. Critics counter that the unresolved problem of long-term waste storage, the high cost of new plants and the lingering fear of accidents make it an unattractive option. Meanwhile, the rapidly falling cost of renewables has shifted the terms of the debate, prompting some to question whether new nuclear capacity is still necessary at all.
dogru: The debate over nuclear power weighs its low-carbon reliability against waste, cost and safety concerns, now complicated by cheaper renewables.
celdiriciler: Both supporters and critics agree that nuclear waste storage has been fully solved.
The falling cost of renewables has made nuclear power the cheapest option.
Critics argue that nuclear power produces large amounts of carbon emissions.

metin: Historians have long debated whether great individuals shape events or are themselves products of their time. Those who emphasise structural forces point to economic conditions, technology and demographic change as the true engines of history. Others insist that particular leaders made decisive choices that could easily have gone otherwise. Most contemporary scholars adopt a middle position, seeing individual agency as operating within, and constrained by, wider circumstances.
dogru: Historians disagree on the role of individuals versus broader forces, and most now see them as interacting.
celdiriciler: Historians unanimously agree that great leaders alone determine the course of history.
Contemporary scholars reject the idea that economic conditions influence history.
The debate about individuals and history was resolved centuries ago.

metin: Open-plan offices were introduced with the promise of fostering collaboration and spontaneous exchanges of ideas. Paradoxically, a number of studies have found that face-to-face interaction declines in such spaces, as employees retreat behind headphones to cope with noise and the feeling of being constantly observed. Email and instant messaging often increase instead. In response, some companies are reintroducing quiet rooms and small enclosed areas for focused work.
dogru: Open-plan offices often fail to increase collaboration, prompting companies to add spaces for focused work.
celdiriciler: Research shows that open-plan offices greatly increase face-to-face conversation.
Employees in open-plan offices send fewer emails and messages.
Companies are removing all quiet rooms to encourage teamwork.

metin: Translation is frequently perceived as a mechanical process of substituting words from one language with their equivalents in another. Experienced translators know otherwise: idioms, cultural references and even the rhythm of a sentence rarely have direct counterparts. A literal rendering may be technically accurate yet entirely miss the tone of the original. Good translation therefore involves countless interpretive decisions, which is why two skilled translators can produce strikingly different versions of the same text.
dogru: Translation involves interpretation rather than simple word substitution, so versions can differ widely.
celdiriciler: Skilled translators always produce identical versions of the same text.
Literal translation reliably preserves the tone of the original.
Idioms and cultural references usually have exact equivalents in other languages.

metin: Economic growth has traditionally been measured by gross domestic product, which captures the total value of goods and services produced. Critics have long pointed out that GDP ignores unpaid work, environmental damage and the distribution of wealth, so a country can grow richer on paper while many of its citizens become worse off. Several governments now publish alternative indicators of well-being alongside GDP, though none has yet displaced it as the dominant measure.
dogru: GDP is criticised as an incomplete measure of progress, and alternatives are emerging without yet replacing it.
celdiriciler: GDP fully accounts for environmental damage and unpaid work.
Governments have abandoned GDP in favour of well-being indicators.
A rising GDP guarantees that every citizen becomes better off.

metin: The migration of songbirds across entire continents has fascinated scientists for centuries. It is now understood that birds navigate using a combination of cues, including the position of the sun, the patterns of stars and the Earth's magnetic field. Recent research suggests that some species may even detect magnetic fields through a chemical reaction in their eyes. How young birds, migrating alone for the first time, acquire this knowledge remains only partly explained.
dogru: Birds use several natural cues to navigate during migration, though some aspects are still not fully understood.
celdiriciler: Scientists have completely explained how young birds learn to migrate.
Songbirds navigate only by following the coastlines.
Research shows that birds cannot sense the Earth's magnetic field.

metin: In an attempt to curb speculation, the city imposed a heavy tax on properties left empty for more than six months. Landlords protested that the measure infringed on their property rights, while housing campaigners welcomed it as overdue. Within a year, several thousand previously vacant flats had returned to the rental market. Whether this will translate into lower rents in the long term remains contested among economists.
dogru: A tax on empty homes increased rental supply, though its long-term effect on rents is uncertain.
celdiriciler: The tax on empty homes was immediately cancelled after protests.
Economists agree that the tax has already lowered rents permanently.
Housing campaigners strongly opposed the new tax.

metin: It is tempting to assume that giving people more choice always makes them happier. Yet psychologists have described a phenomenon sometimes called choice overload: when faced with an excessive number of options, people may delay decisions, feel less satisfied with what they eventually choose, or avoid choosing altogether. Retailers who reduced the range of products on display have occasionally seen their sales rise as a result.
dogru: Too many options can make decisions harder and less satisfying.
celdiriciler: More choice always leads to greater happiness and satisfaction.
Retailers increase sales by displaying as many products as possible.
People make decisions faster when they have many options.

metin: Few architectural styles have provoked as much controversy as brutalism, with its exposed concrete and uncompromising geometric forms. Built largely in the decades after the Second World War, many brutalist buildings were intended to express social ideals, housing families or providing public services on a large scale. For years they were widely derided as ugly and oppressive, and many were demolished. Recently, however, a new generation has begun to champion them as bold and honest works of design.
dogru: Brutalist architecture, once widely disliked and often demolished, is being reappraised by a new generation.
celdiriciler: Brutalist buildings have always been universally admired.
Brutalism was mainly used for luxury private homes before the war.
Younger people are campaigning to demolish all brutalist buildings.

metin: When the pharmaceutical company announced that its new drug had succeeded in clinical trials, its share price soared. Independent researchers, however, noted that the trial had been relatively small and that the benefits, while statistically significant, were modest in practical terms. They cautioned against headlines describing the drug as a breakthrough. Such episodes illustrate the gap that can open up between scientific findings and the way they are communicated.
dogru: The case shows how modest scientific results can be exaggerated in the way they are reported.
celdiriciler: Independent researchers described the drug as a major breakthrough.
The clinical trial was very large and showed dramatic benefits.
The company's share price fell after the announcement.

metin: The concept of the 'digital native', a young person who has grown up with technology and is therefore naturally skilled with it, has shaped educational policy for years. Empirical studies, however, have cast doubt on this assumption. Many young people are adept at using social media and games but struggle to evaluate the reliability of online information or to use software for complex tasks. Educators increasingly argue that digital skills must be taught explicitly rather than taken for granted.
dogru: Young people are not automatically skilled with technology, so digital skills need to be taught.
celdiriciler: Studies confirm that all young people are expert users of technology.
Young people are especially good at evaluating online information.
Educators recommend removing digital skills from the curriculum.

metin: Ancient Rome is often celebrated for its engineering achievements, from aqueducts to paved roads that still survive today. Less frequently discussed is the fact that Roman concrete appears to be more durable than many modern equivalents, particularly in seawater. Researchers have discovered that certain minerals in the Roman mixture continue to form over time, effectively strengthening the material. Engineers are now investigating whether similar principles could be applied to modern construction.
dogru: The unusual durability of Roman concrete is inspiring research into modern building materials.
celdiriciler: Roman concrete was much weaker than modern concrete.
Seawater quickly destroyed all Roman concrete structures.
Engineers have decided that Roman techniques have no modern use.

metin: For much of the twentieth century, dietary advice focused on reducing fat, and the food industry responded with a wave of low-fat products. Many of these, however, compensated for the loss of flavour by adding sugar. Nutritional science has since moved towards a more nuanced view, distinguishing between different types of fats and paying closer attention to the effects of refined carbohydrates. The episode is often cited as a cautionary tale about simplifying complex evidence.
dogru: Oversimplified advice to reduce fat led to sugary products, and nutritional science has since become more nuanced.
celdiriciler: Low-fat products were generally lower in sugar than normal products.
Nutritional science still treats all fats as equally harmful.
The food industry ignored twentieth-century dietary advice.

metin: Emerging from years of civil conflict, the country faced the daunting task of rebuilding trust between communities that had fought each other. Rather than relying solely on criminal trials, the government established commissions where victims could tell their stories and perpetrators could acknowledge their actions. Such processes are imperfect and often frustrating for those seeking justice, but they have been credited with helping societies move forward without renewed violence.
dogru: After a civil conflict, truth-telling commissions were used alongside trials to help rebuild trust.
celdiriciler: The government refused to address the crimes committed during the conflict.
The commissions satisfied every victim's desire for justice.
Criminal trials were the only method used to rebuild trust.

metin: Gig economy platforms describe their workers as independent contractors who enjoy the freedom to choose when and how much they work. Labour organisations, however, argue that many drivers and couriers are economically dependent on a single platform and subject to algorithmic control over their pay and conduct. Courts in several countries have ruled that such workers should be entitled to minimum wages and holiday pay, although the legal picture remains fragmented.
dogru: The status of gig workers is disputed, and some courts have granted them employment rights.
celdiriciler: All courts agree that gig workers are fully independent contractors.
Gig workers have complete control over their pay and working conditions.
Labour organisations support the platforms' view of their workers.

metin: Memory is not a faithful recording of the past but a reconstruction that can be altered each time it is recalled. Experiments have shown that people can be led to 'remember' events that never happened, simply through suggestive questioning. These findings have serious implications for the legal system, where eyewitness testimony has traditionally carried great weight. Several wrongful convictions have been overturned after it emerged that witnesses' memories had been unintentionally distorted.
dogru: Because memory is reconstructive and can be distorted, eyewitness testimony may be unreliable.
celdiriciler: Human memory works like an accurate video recording.
Suggestive questioning cannot change people's memories.
Eyewitness testimony has never led to a wrongful conviction.

metin: The rapid expansion of desalination plants has been hailed as a solution to water scarcity in arid regions. Converting seawater into drinking water, however, requires considerable amounts of energy, and the process produces a highly concentrated brine that is often discharged back into the sea, where it can harm marine ecosystems. Researchers are exploring ways to use renewable energy and to find commercial uses for the brine, but these solutions are not yet widespread.
dogru: Desalination helps with water shortages but has energy and environmental drawbacks that are not yet solved.
celdiriciler: Desalination uses very little energy and produces no waste.
The brine from desalination is harmless to marine life.
Desalination plants are being closed because water scarcity has ended.

metin: Minority languages are disappearing at an alarming rate, with linguists estimating that a significant proportion of the world's languages may vanish this century. When a language dies, it takes with it unique ways of describing the world, from specialised knowledge of local plants to oral histories. Revitalisation efforts, such as immersion schools and digital dictionaries, have had notable successes, but they depend heavily on the commitment of younger speakers.
dogru: Many languages are endangered, and their survival depends on revitalisation efforts supported by young speakers.
celdiriciler: The number of languages in the world is increasing rapidly.
When a language disappears, no knowledge is lost.
Revitalisation efforts have never succeeded anywhere.

metin: The novelist spent a decade working on her latest book, repeatedly abandoning drafts that failed to satisfy her. In interviews, she has described the process as less a matter of inspiration than of endurance: writing each morning regardless of mood, and accepting that most of what she produced would be discarded. Critics have praised the finished novel as her most accomplished work, suggesting that the long gestation was worthwhile.
dogru: The novelist's persistent, disciplined work over many years produced a highly praised book.
celdiriciler: The novelist wrote her book quickly in a burst of inspiration.
Critics considered the novel her weakest work.
The novelist only wrote when she felt inspired.

metin: Microplastics, fragments smaller than five millimetres, have now been detected in environments as remote as mountain snow and deep-sea sediments, as well as in drinking water and human tissue. Their effects on human health are not yet well understood, partly because they are so varied in size and chemical composition. Scientists stress the need for further research, while some policymakers argue that precautionary measures should not wait for definitive evidence.
dogru: Microplastics are found almost everywhere, and their health effects remain uncertain.
celdiriciler: Microplastics have only been found in heavily polluted cities.
Scientists have fully established that microplastics are harmless.
Policymakers agree that nothing should be done until research is complete.

metin: When the museum announced that it would return a collection of artefacts to the country from which they had been taken during the colonial period, reactions were sharply divided. Some praised the decision as a long-overdue act of justice. Others worried that it would set a precedent leading to the emptying of Western museums. The debate reflects broader questions about who owns cultural heritage and who has the right to tell its story.
dogru: A museum's decision to return colonial-era artefacts sparked debate about the ownership of cultural heritage.
celdiriciler: The museum decided to buy more artefacts from former colonies.
Everyone agreed that returning the artefacts was the right decision.
The artefacts had been legally purchased at fair prices.

metin: Conventional wisdom holds that financial incentives reliably improve performance. For simple, mechanical tasks this is often true. Yet experiments have repeatedly found that for tasks requiring creative thinking, large bonuses can actually impair performance, perhaps because the pressure narrows attention. Some organisations have consequently shifted towards giving employees greater autonomy and a sense of purpose rather than relying primarily on monetary rewards.
dogru: Financial rewards help with simple tasks but may harm creative work, so some firms emphasise autonomy and purpose.
celdiriciler: Large bonuses always improve performance in creative tasks.
Money has no effect on performance in any kind of task.
Organisations are increasing bonuses and reducing employee autonomy.

metin: Satellite data have revolutionised our ability to monitor deforestation, allowing scientists to detect illegal logging in near real time. However, the availability of information has not always translated into action. Enforcement depends on political will, adequate funding and cooperation with local communities, all of which may be lacking. Some of the most successful programmes have combined satellite monitoring with legal recognition of indigenous land rights.
dogru: Satellite monitoring of deforestation is powerful, but it only works when combined with effective action on the ground.
celdiriciler: Satellite data have completely stopped illegal logging.
Governments cannot detect deforestation until years later.
Indigenous land rights have made deforestation worse.

metin: The placebo effect, in which patients improve after receiving a treatment with no active ingredient, has long been regarded as a nuisance in clinical trials. Intriguingly, recent studies have found that placebos can sometimes work even when patients are told they are taking a placebo. Researchers suggest that the ritual of treatment and the expectation of care may themselves trigger measurable changes in the body, particularly for conditions such as pain.
dogru: Placebos can have real effects, sometimes even when patients know they are receiving one.
celdiriciler: Placebos only work when patients are deceived about them.
Researchers have proved that the placebo effect does not exist.
Placebos contain powerful active ingredients.

metin: In the early years of the internet, many hoped it would democratise access to knowledge and foster informed public debate. While it has indeed made vast amounts of information freely available, it has also enabled the rapid spread of misinformation and the formation of isolated communities in which people encounter only views that confirm their own. Scholars remain divided over how far these effects are caused by technology itself rather than by pre-existing social divisions.
dogru: The internet has spread knowledge but also misinformation, and experts disagree about technology's exact role in this.
celdiriciler: The internet has made no difference to access to information.
Scholars agree that technology alone causes social divisions.
Misinformation spreads more slowly online than offline.

metin: After the factory that had employed much of the town for generations closed down, unemployment soared and many young people left. Instead of waiting for a new major employer, local leaders invested in training programmes and encouraged small start-ups, some housed in the old factory buildings. Progress has been slow and uneven, but the town's population has stabilised and a modest number of new jobs have appeared.
dogru: After losing its main employer, a town slowly recovered by supporting training and small businesses.
celdiriciler: A new large factory immediately replaced the one that closed.
The town's population has continued to fall sharply.
The old factory buildings were demolished and left empty.

metin: Dreams have been interpreted as divine messages, expressions of repressed desires and random by-products of brain activity. Contemporary neuroscience has not settled the question of why we dream, but it has shown that dreaming is associated with specific sleep stages and may play a role in consolidating memories and processing emotions. Some researchers are cautious, however, noting that correlation does not necessarily imply that dreams serve a function.
dogru: The purpose of dreaming is still debated, though research links it to memory and emotion.
celdiriciler: Neuroscience has definitively proved why we dream.
Dreams occur equally in all stages of sleep.
Researchers agree that dreams have no connection to memory.

metin: The introduction of congestion charges in several major cities was initially met with fierce opposition from businesses and drivers. Where the charges were implemented, traffic generally fell and public transport use rose, and in some cases public support increased once the benefits became visible. Nonetheless, critics argue that such charges disproportionately affect lower-income residents who depend on their cars and have few alternatives.
dogru: Congestion charges have reduced traffic and gained support, though concerns about fairness remain.
celdiriciler: Congestion charges increased traffic in city centres.
Businesses strongly supported congestion charges from the start.
Critics say congestion charges mainly affect wealthy residents.

metin: For centuries, sailors dreaded scurvy, a disease that could kill a large proportion of a ship's crew on long voyages. Although citrus fruit had been observed to prevent the illness as early as the seventeenth century, the knowledge was repeatedly forgotten or dismissed in favour of other theories. It was not until much later that the role of vitamin C was understood. The story is often used to show how valuable evidence can be overlooked when it conflicts with prevailing beliefs.
dogru: Knowledge that citrus prevented scurvy was repeatedly ignored, showing how evidence can be overlooked.
celdiriciler: Scurvy was a minor illness that rarely affected sailors.
The cure for scurvy was accepted immediately and never forgotten.
Vitamin C was understood before sailors began long voyages.

metin: Large-scale infrastructure projects are notorious for running over budget and behind schedule. Researchers who have analysed hundreds of such projects argue that the problem lies less in unforeseeable events than in systematic optimism: planners underestimate costs and overestimate benefits, sometimes deliberately in order to secure approval. They recommend comparing new projects with the actual outcomes of similar past ones rather than relying on detailed internal forecasts.
dogru: Infrastructure projects often overrun because of systematic optimism, which can be reduced by comparing with past projects.
celdiriciler: Most infrastructure projects finish early and under budget.
Cost overruns are caused mainly by unpredictable natural disasters.
Researchers recommend relying only on internal forecasts.

metin: Although she had written dozens of scientific papers, the researcher found that few people outside her field understood her work on soil microbes. She began writing a blog in plain language and giving talks at local schools and farmers' markets. To her surprise, several farmers contacted her with questions that led to new research collaborations. She now argues that public engagement is not a distraction from science but a vital part of it.
dogru: Communicating her research to the public led a scientist to valuable new collaborations.
celdiriciler: The researcher stopped publishing scientific papers to write a blog.
Farmers showed no interest in the researcher's work.
The researcher believes public engagement distracts from real science.

metin: Urban agriculture, from rooftop gardens to vertical farms in converted warehouses, has attracted growing interest as cities seek to shorten supply chains. Enthusiasts highlight fresher produce and reduced transport emissions. Sceptics point out that vertical farms consume large amounts of electricity for lighting and are currently viable mainly for high-value crops such as herbs and salad leaves. Staple foods like grain are unlikely ever to be grown on a meaningful scale in cities.
dogru: Urban farming has benefits but significant limits, particularly for energy use and staple crops.
celdiriciler: Vertical farms use very little electricity.
Cities will soon produce most of the world's grain.
Urban agriculture increases transport emissions.

metin: The four-hundred-year-old manuscript had been catalogued as an anonymous work until a doctoral student noticed striking similarities between its handwriting and letters written by a well-known scholar of the period. Further analysis of the paper and ink supported her hypothesis. If confirmed, the attribution would significantly alter our understanding of the scholar's intellectual development, as the manuscript contains ideas previously thought to have emerged only later in his career.
dogru: A student's discovery may identify the author of an old manuscript and change views of a scholar's development.
celdiriciler: The manuscript's author has been known for four hundred years.
Analysis of the paper and ink disproved the student's theory.
The manuscript contains only ideas the scholar developed late in life.

metin: The term 'burnout' was originally used to describe exhaustion among workers in caring professions, such as nurses and social workers. It is now applied far more broadly, sometimes to the point where critics fear it has lost its precise meaning. Researchers typically define it by three features: emotional exhaustion, a growing cynicism towards one's work and a sense of reduced effectiveness. Crucially, they regard it as a response to chronic workplace conditions rather than a personal weakness.
dogru: Burnout is a specific response to chronic work conditions, although the term is now used loosely.
celdiriciler: Burnout is considered a sign of personal weakness by researchers.
The term burnout has always been used only for office workers.
Burnout is defined simply as feeling tired after a long day.

metin: Coral reefs occupy a tiny fraction of the ocean floor yet support around a quarter of all marine species. Rising sea temperatures cause corals to expel the algae that provide them with food and colour, a process known as bleaching. If temperatures return to normal quickly, corals can recover, but repeated bleaching events leave little time for this. Scientists are experimenting with breeding more heat-tolerant corals, though they emphasise that this cannot substitute for reducing emissions.
dogru: Warming seas threaten coral reefs through repeated bleaching, and breeding tougher corals is not a substitute for cutting emissions.
celdiriciler: Coral reefs support only a very small number of marine species.
Bleached corals can never recover under any conditions.
Scientists believe heat-tolerant corals make reducing emissions unnecessary.

metin: The debate over whether homework benefits young children has been surprisingly persistent. Meta-analyses suggest that the academic benefits for primary school pupils are small, while the costs, in terms of family stress and reduced time for play, may be considerable. For older students, the relationship between homework and achievement appears stronger. Some primary schools have therefore replaced traditional homework with encouragement to read for pleasure.
dogru: Homework seems to help older students more than young children, leading some primary schools to change their approach.
celdiriciler: Research shows homework greatly benefits young children.
Homework has no connection with achievement for older students.
Primary schools are giving more homework than ever.

metin: Initially dismissed as a passing fashion, the cooperative café was founded by a group of young people who pooled their savings and agreed to share decisions and profits equally. Running a business collectively proved harder than expected: meetings were long, and disagreements about priorities were frequent. Over time, they developed clearer roles while preserving equal ownership. Five years on, the café has opened a second branch.
dogru: Despite early difficulties, a cooperative café adapted its organisation and grew.
celdiriciler: The cooperative café closed after its first year.
The founders abandoned equal ownership to make decisions faster.
Running the café collectively was easy from the beginning.

metin: Critics of standardised testing argue that it narrows the curriculum, encouraging teachers to focus on what is examined at the expense of creativity and critical thinking. Defenders respond that tests provide an objective means of holding schools accountable and identifying pupils who need extra support. Both sides tend to agree that the problems arise mainly when a single test carries excessive consequences for students, teachers or schools.
dogru: Standardised tests have both critics and defenders, who largely agree that high stakes are the main problem.
celdiriciler: Both sides agree that standardised tests should be abolished.
Defenders claim that tests encourage creativity above all.
Critics believe tests widen the curriculum.

metin: Plans to build a wind farm off the coast divided the fishing community. Some fishermen feared the turbines would disrupt fishing grounds, while others hoped for compensation and new jobs in maintenance. Through a lengthy consultation, the developers adjusted the layout to avoid the most important areas and created a fund for local projects. The compromise did not satisfy everyone, but it allowed construction to proceed with broader support.
dogru: Consultation led to a compromise that allowed a wind farm to be built with wider local support.
celdiriciler: All fishermen enthusiastically supported the wind farm from the start.
The developers refused to change their plans in any way.
The wind farm project was cancelled after the consultation.

metin: Language shapes, to some extent, the way we perceive the world, although the strong claim that it determines thought has largely been abandoned. Studies of speakers of languages with different colour terms, for instance, suggest small differences in how quickly colours are distinguished. Similarly, languages that describe directions in absolute terms, such as north and south, rather than left and right, appear to encourage remarkable spatial orientation among their speakers.
dogru: Language appears to influence perception in modest ways, though it does not determine thought.
celdiriciler: Research proves that language completely determines how we think.
Languages have no effect at all on how speakers perceive colours.
Speakers of languages using north and south have poor spatial orientation.

metin: Crowdfunding platforms have enabled countless artists, inventors and charities to raise money directly from the public. Success stories are widely publicised, yet the majority of campaigns fail to reach their targets, and a significant number of funded projects never deliver what they promised. Platforms generally accept little responsibility in such cases. Analysts advise backers to treat contributions more as support for an idea than as a guaranteed purchase.
dogru: Crowdfunding offers opportunities but carries risks, so backers should not expect guaranteed results.
celdiriciler: Most crowdfunding campaigns easily reach their targets.
Platforms guarantee that every funded project will be delivered.
Backing a crowdfunding project is the same as buying a product in a shop.

metin: Advances in genetic testing now allow individuals to learn about their ancestry and potential health risks from a simple saliva sample. These services raise complex ethical questions. Results about disease risk can cause anxiety without clear guidance on what to do, and genetic information reveals details not only about the person tested but also about their relatives, who have not given consent. Regulation has struggled to keep pace with the technology.
dogru: Consumer genetic testing raises ethical issues about anxiety, consent and regulation.
celdiriciler: Genetic tests reveal information only about the person tested.
Regulation of genetic testing is well ahead of the technology.
Genetic tests require a complicated medical operation.

metin: The orchestra, facing declining audiences and rising costs, took the unusual step of performing in unconventional venues such as factories, hospitals and railway stations. Musicians initially had reservations about the acoustics and the informal atmosphere. The experiment, however, attracted many people who had never attended a classical concert, and a noticeable number of them subsequently bought tickets for performances in the concert hall.
dogru: Performing in unusual places helped an orchestra reach new audiences.
celdiriciler: The orchestra stopped performing because of rising costs.
The musicians were enthusiastic about the acoustics from the beginning.
The new audiences never attended the concert hall afterwards.

metin: Invasive species, introduced intentionally or accidentally into new environments, can have devastating consequences for native wildlife. Without natural predators, they may multiply rapidly and outcompete local species for food and space. Eradication programmes are costly and succeed mainly on small islands. Consequently, conservationists increasingly emphasise prevention, such as stricter controls on the transport of plants and animals across borders.
dogru: Because invasive species are hard to eradicate, conservation efforts focus increasingly on prevention.
celdiriciler: Invasive species usually help native wildlife to thrive.
Eradication programmes are cheap and succeed everywhere.
Conservationists want fewer controls on transporting animals.

metin: The ideal of objectivity has long been central to journalism, requiring reporters to present facts without taking sides. Some contemporary journalists question whether complete objectivity is achievable, since choices about which stories to cover and whom to interview inevitably reflect certain values. They propose transparency about methods and perspectives as a more honest standard. Others fear that abandoning objectivity would further erode public trust in the media.
dogru: Journalists debate whether objectivity is possible or whether transparency is a better standard.
celdiriciler: All journalists agree that complete objectivity is easy to achieve.
Choosing which stories to cover involves no values at all.
Public trust in the media depends only on transparency.

metin: Although Ottoman coffeehouses are often remembered as places of leisure, historians have shown that they also served as important centres of news, political discussion and cultural life. Authorities periodically attempted to close them, fearing they encouraged dissent. Storytellers performed there, and in some periods, newspapers were read aloud to customers who could not read. Their role has been compared to that of European salons and cafés in the spread of public opinion.
dogru: Ottoman coffeehouses were important centres of news and discussion, not merely places of leisure.
celdiriciler: Ottoman coffeehouses were used only for drinking coffee quietly.
Authorities always encouraged political discussion in coffeehouses.
Newspapers were never available in Ottoman coffeehouses.

metin: The pandemic forced universities to shift to online teaching almost overnight. Many lecturers who had resisted digital tools discovered unexpected advantages, such as the ability to reach students unable to travel. Yet surveys also revealed widespread feelings of isolation among students and difficulties in maintaining motivation. As a result, most institutions have settled on hybrid models that aim to retain the flexibility of online learning without sacrificing personal contact.
dogru: Online teaching during the pandemic had benefits and drawbacks, leading to hybrid models.
celdiriciler: Universities returned to purely traditional teaching and abandoned digital tools.
Students reported feeling more connected than ever during online teaching.
Lecturers found no advantages in online teaching.

metin: Mountaineers attempting the world's highest peaks now face a problem that early climbers could hardly have imagined: overcrowding. On days with favourable weather, long queues can form near the summit, forcing climbers to wait at altitudes where the body deteriorates rapidly. Several deaths have been attributed to these delays. Some experts call for stricter permit systems and minimum experience requirements, though such measures would affect the incomes of local guides.
dogru: Overcrowding on high peaks has become dangerous, but proposed restrictions have economic consequences.
celdiriciler: Queues on high mountains have no effect on climbers' safety.
Early climbers often complained about crowds at the summit.
Stricter permits would increase the income of local guides.

metin: The long-standing assumption that intelligence is fixed at birth has been challenged by research on neuroplasticity, which shows that the brain continues to form new connections throughout life. Educational psychologists have drawn on this work to argue that students who believe their abilities can grow tend to persist longer with difficult tasks. Subsequent attempts to replicate some of these findings, however, have produced smaller effects than originally reported.
dogru: Research suggests abilities can develop, though some related findings have proved weaker than first claimed.
celdiriciler: Neuroplasticity research proves that intelligence is fixed at birth.
The brain stops forming new connections after childhood.
All attempts to replicate the findings produced larger effects.

metin: In recent decades, the global middle class has expanded dramatically, particularly in Asia, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. This transformation has also increased demand for meat, cars and air travel, placing additional pressure on the environment. Economists debate whether technological innovation can decouple rising living standards from environmental harm quickly enough, or whether more fundamental changes in consumption patterns will be required.
dogru: The growth of the global middle class has reduced poverty but increased environmental pressure, raising questions about the future.
celdiriciler: The global middle class has shrunk in recent decades.
Rising living standards have reduced demand for meat and air travel.
Economists agree that technology has already solved the environmental impact of growth.
